==English== {{wp}} ===Pronunciation=== * {{enPR|fäst|a=RP,AU,NZ,South Africa}}, {{IPA|en|/fɑːst/}} ** {{audio|en|en-uk-fast.ogg|a=RP}} ** {{rhymes|en|ɑːst|s=1}} * {{enPR|făst|a=Northern England,GA,CA}}, {{IPA|en|/fæst/}} ** {{audio|en|en-us-fast.ogg|a=US}} ** {{rhymes|en|æst|s=1}} ===Etymology 1=== {{etymon|en|id=adjective|:inh|enm:fast>|tree=1}} {{root|en|ine-pro|*peh₂ǵ-}} From {{inh|en|enm|fast}}, {{m|enm|fest}}, from {{inh|en|ang|fæst|t=firm, secure}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*fast}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*fastuz}}; see it for cognates and further etymology. The development of “rapid” from an original sense of “secure” apparently happened first in the adverb and then transferred to the adjective; compare {{m|en|hard}} in expressions like “to run hard”. The original sense of “secure, firm” is now slightly archaic, but retained in the related {{m|en|fasten|t=make secure}}. Also compare close meaning change from {{noncog|la|rapiō|t=to snatch}} to {{noncog|la|rapidus|t=rapid, quick}}, from {{noncog|ga|sciob|t=to snatch}} to {{noncog|ga|sciobtha|t=quick}}. ====Adjective==== {{en-adj|er}} # {{lb|en|dated}} [[firmly|Firmly]] or [[securely]] fixed in place; [[stable]]. {{defdate|from 9th c.}} #: {{syn|en|firm|immobile|secure|stable|stuck|tight}} #: {{ant|en|loose}} #: {{hypo|en|bedfast|chairfast|colorfast|fail-fast|lightfast|shamefast|soothfast|steadfast}} #: {{ux|en|That rope is dangerously loose. {{tt+|ru|преждевременно}} * Swahili: * Swedish: {{trans-bottom}} }} ===Etymology 3=== From {{inh|en|enm|fasten}}, from {{inh|en|ang|fæstan|t=to fast}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*fastēn}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*fastāną|t=to fast}}, from the same root as {{inh|en|gem-pro|*fastijaną|t=to fasten}}, derived from {{m|gem-pro|*fastuz}}, and thereby related to Etymology 1. The religious sense is presumably introduced in the Gothic church, from {{cog|got|𐍆𐌰𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌽||hold fast (viz. to the rule of abstinence)}}. This semantic development is unique to Gothic, the term glosses Greek {{m|grc|νηστεύω}}, Latin {{m|la|ieiuno}} which do not have similar connotations of "holding fast". The feminine noun {{cog|goh|fasta}} likely existed in the 8th century (shift to neuter {{cog|goh|fasten}} from the 9th century, whence modern {{cog|de|Fasten}}). The Old English noun originally had the sense "fortress, enclosure" and takes the religious sense only in late Old English, perhaps influenced by {{der|en|non|fasta}}. The use for reduced nutrition intake for medical reasons or for weight reduction develops by the mid-1970s, back-formed from the use of the verbal noun {{m|en|fasting}} in this sense (1960s). ====Verb==== {{en-verb}} # {{lb|en|intransitive}} To practice religious abstinence, especially from food. #* {{RQ:KJV|2 Samuel|12|21|passage=Thou didst '''fast''' and weep for the child.}} #* {{RQ:Milton Paradise Regained|2|passage='''Fasting''' he went to sleep, and '''fasting''' waked.}} # {{lb|en|intransitive}} To reduce or limit one's nutrition intake for medical or health reasons, to [[diet]]. #* {{quote-journal|en|year=1977|author=Suza Norton|title=To get the most benefit from fasting use a body-building diet|journal=Yoga Journal|section=Jul-Aug 1977, p. 40 |passage=The ideal would be to '''fast''' in a situation where you are not tempted by food}} #* {{quote-book|en|year=1983|title=Experimental Lung Research|volume=5-6|publisher=Informa healthcare|page=134 |passage=After the equilibration period, the rats designated for deprivation studies were made to '''fast''' for 24, 48, 72, or 96 hr according to experimental design.}} #
